events.title: Ùna nic Choinnich calls the guild to the hall
events.body: The agent of A' Chompanaidh at Muileann chrom sends notice to Muileann chiar that surveyors will measure the silver seam in spring under the charter's first refusal. Ùna nic Choinnich reads the letter in both tongues to forty-one members of Comann an Airgid gathered in the guild hall by night, and resolves to ask the council what it holds.

events.title: Coinneach Glas lends Ùna the council's copies
events.body: Ùna nic Choinnich rides three days to Cathair dhearg. Coinneach Glas, Ceann a' Chùraim, aged sixty-eight and ailing, hears her out in the room of the rolls and gives her the council's own copies of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, Puingean a' Chalaidh and the pit contracts, bidding her look for the silver before the humans do.

events.title: Ùna finds no silver in Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg
events.body: Reading the council's copies by rushlight at the inns of Rathad na Mèinne on her way home, Ùna nic Choinnich finds coal named on every page of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg and no word of silver, nor of any metal but the iron the humans paid with. At the inn below Muileann chrom she tells her grandson that A' Chompanaidh holds no paper for the seam.

events.title: The surveyor's report reaches Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
events.body: The chief surveyor reports to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that the whole of Muileann chiar met him at the working, silent, and that he found no grant or payment to A' Chompanaidh in either of the guild's books and did not think it prudent to proceed. Lisle writes beneath it that he would not have found it either, and sends for the bound book.

events.title: Lisle writes that the charter gives A' Chompanaidh nothing
events.body: In a long letter to the master of A' Chompanaidh, Arthur Lisle sets out that Cairt na Companaidh is a promise made by its own masters and grants nothing on the island, where the only title is Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, which speaks of coal and says nothing of silver. The master of A' Chompanaidh protests; Lisle answers in two lines.

events.title: The council's copies returned from Muileann chiar
events.body: In the spring after the compact Ùna nic Choinnich sends the council's leaves of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, Puingean a' Chalaidh and the pit contracts back to Cathair dhearg by her grandson Fionnlagh, wrapped in the same oilcloth they came in, with a bar of silver for the clerk who keeps the presses.

events.title: Ùna locks the compact in the guild chest
events.body: On the day Comann an Airgid reckons its year, the three keyholders open the guild chest and Cùmhnant an Airgid is read aloud in both tongues. Ùna nic Choinnich, aged fifty-nine, lays it back on the new book of weighings beside the notched boards of the old ledger, and the three locks are turned.

events.title: The keeper of Àth dhearg sees the burning collier
events.body: Two nights after entering a laden collier of A' Chompanaidh going south, Tormod mac Pheadair sees a red light low in the south under the cloud from the middle watch until near dawn, and writes that he does not know what it was. The carters bring word four days later that raiders have burned her.

events.title: A' Chompanaidh charges Comann an Airgid with the burning
events.body: Within a month of the burning the agents of A' Chompanaidh say at Seann Bhral and Ros dhomhain, and write to Arthur Lisle, that Comann an Airgid paid the raiders in spite for the surveyors turned back from the adit at Muileann chiar. The guild makes no answer.

events.title: The keeper will not write the black boats
events.body: In Dubhlas a clerk of A' Chompanaidh rides to Àth dhearg to read the daybook and asks the keeper to write in black raiding boats seen going south before the burning. Tormod mac Pheadair answers that he saw none and will write no boat he has not seen. The clerk reports the book of no assistance.

events.title: The gunboat entered at Àth dhearg
events.body: In Teasach of the forty-seventh year a black two-masted ship of war of A' Chompanaidh, a gun in her bows under canvas and more men on deck than any trader carries, comes round the north coast and south past the cape. The keeper of Àth dhearg enters her with more care than any ship before.

events.title: The wall's footing on the shingle of Baile dhìreach
events.body: Promised timber by A' Chompanaidh, the yard-master Daniel Lusk asks the council of four at Baile dhìreach for a dry-stone wall up the town's shingle and lays its footing while they argue. The town's members hold that the shingle is kept and not built on. On the third night the stones are carried below the wrack-line.

events.title: Iain Hale refuses the yard at Inis chrom
events.body: Daniel Lusk offers Iain Hale the foreman's place in the yard going to Inis chrom, for more marks than the yard has ever paid. After a night on the shingle and a talk with his father, Iain Hale refuses, and that winter builds the town's boats on the old slip by the town's leave.

events.title: The rain fails in the Àth dhearg daybook
events.body: Through the spring and summer of the forty-eighth year the daybook of Àth dhearg records dry winds night after night, the fields inland yellow before midsummer, a heath fire of three days, and the burn below the town stopped, which it has never done in memory. Rain is written once in four months.

events.title: Aonghas mac Coinnich writes the question in the register
events.body: At midsummer Aonghas mac Coinnich, master of the house of disputation at Dùn thais, tips a basket of the Company's broken coal onto his table and has his students name its colours. He writes his question in the register in his own hand. Seumas mac Artair, keeper of the register, sets down below it that the master called it the wrong question and would not give the right one.

events.title: Eachann Mòr loses his seat
events.body: The council at Cathair dhearg protests the charter of Cathair gheal, which names no custodian, and receives an answer in the humans' tongue that none of its members can read with confidence. At the autumn choosing at Ceann àrsaidh the households put out Eachann Mòr, who has no letters of that tongue, and choose Dùghall Òg of the carting families, who worked five years at the Company's weigh-house.

events.title: Calum's ship sails north-about
events.body: Calum, son of Eachann Mòr, thirteen years old, goes aboard a Company ship at the quay below the Residency at Ros dhomhain with the Mission's letter and a purse of marks sewn into his coat. A pilot of Caol leathan takes her down the Abhainn gheal on the evening tide, and she turns north up the west coast to go round by the north to the humans' land.

events.title: Eachann Mòr's first letter over the sea
events.body: No letter comes from Calum by the autumn ships. In the winter Eachann Mòr writes to his son in Dia-thìris, pays a pupil of the Mission school to put it into the humans' tongue beneath his lines, and gives it with a mark to the master of the first ship going north. No answer comes to it, nor to the three he sends after it.

events.title: Ciorstaidh nic Eachainn at the school of Inis bhàn
events.body: Eachann Mòr sends his daughter Ciorstaidh, ten years old, to the custodians' new school at Inis bhàn. She comes home at midsummer able to name forty hills and to argue the boundaries of her father's parish. The custodians of Inis bhàn keep the Mission's complaint about their pupils as a testimonial.

events.title: The students at Drochaid Ros fhionn
events.body: Aonghas mac Coinnich takes the students of Dùn thais to watch the first coal-carts cross the rebuilt bridge at Ros fhionn, forty in an afternoon. The island's drivers throw down lumps for them to name; the two human drivers look at their loads as at stones. Ailean Clachair's sign stays in the keystone.

events.title: The passenger line read at the Company's counter
events.body: In the third year after his son sailed Eachann Mòr asks at the Company's counter at Ros dhomhain after the ship by name. She has come and gone twice since, under another master now. Against the day Calum sailed the clerk reads one line, a native boy, his fare paid in full, and says his book knows nothing more.

events.title: Barabal nic Dhùghaill reads the schedule at Cathair dhearg
events.body: A Mission pupil of fifteen, Barabal nic Dhùghaill, renders Lisle's three sealed sheets into Dia-thìris before the council, reading the new fraction twice over at the old custodian of Cnoc bheag's asking. The council has her rendering copied word for word into every coal town's roll, with her own name set at the foot of each copy.

events.title: Mòr nic Amhlaidh's counsel on names
events.body: Washing the chapel floor by lamplight on Colby's first night of nursing the flux, the widow Mòr nic Amhlaidh tells her that the dying want their own names said to them more than they want the fever broken. Colby is said to have kept the counsel from that night on.

events.title: The Company's surgeon visits once
events.body: The Company's own surgeon comes to the chapel door at Ros dhomhain, will not step past the threshold, and tells Colby she would do better to let the sick lie where they were found. He sends, before he leaves the harbour, a case of salts and does not come again.

events.title: Colby's roll of the dead by name
events.body: Each evening Anne Colby sits at the chapel door with the custodians' own roll open on her knee and a clerk's boy to read her the entries, and sets down against every name who lived and who died, in English, in a column she turns round on the table for the custodians to see is kept.

events.title: Uisdean Ruadh's first walk to Ceann mhin
events.body: Uisdean Ruadh, a hewer of Muileann chrom, walks with forty of his gang before light on a morning of frost to stand in the pay line at Ceann mhin till near dusk, and walks home again in the dark. He keeps the cost of it afterward on a notched stick, kept still by his family three generations on.

events.title: Raghnall Maor dies at Muileann chrom
events.body: Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, called Raghnall Maor, dies at two and seventy in the slate-roofed house the Company built him above the pit he first walked as a guide. Anne Colby, sent for by his son, sits with him two nights before the end; he asks her once whether she writes her dead down by name and tells her it is a good thing to keep doing.

events.title: Raghnall Maor buried beside the eleven
events.body: Raghnall Maor is buried on the hill above Muileann chrom beside the eleven of his first gallery, in thin rain, with both shifts of the pit standing at the grave together, a thing not done for any death there before. Anne Colby stands at the grave's edge with her roll and adds, that evening, a line naming his office, the only such line the roll holds.
